title: Getting around
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE IMPERATIVE IS FREE HERE: the vous imperative is the present tense with the pronoun taken off. vous tournez → Tournez, vous allez → Allez, vous prenez → Prenez. Every one of those present forms is already the learner's, so this module's grammar costs nothing and the whole budget goes to the prepositions and the words. The tu imperative — tourne, va, prends — exists and is not written, because the scene is a stranger in the street.

TRANSPORT SPLITS ON ONE RELIABLE RULE: EN for anything you get inside — en bus, en train, en voiture, en avion — and À for anything you sit on or use with your body: à pied, à vélo, à moto. That one really is a rule and not a list, which makes it the cheapest thing in the module.

droite is "right" and tout droit is "straight on". One letter apart, and a whole different direction. A learner who hears them as the same word will turn where they should not, so the module puts them in one sentence and spends a mistake block on the pair.

à gauche and à droite are taught WHOLE. That keeps L1-M4's à on its own row and gives the direction its own note — there is nothing to assemble here, and a learner who tries will get the article wrong.

il faut is a FROZEN impersonal plus an infinitive: Il faut tourner à gauche. It is the most useful obligation frame in the language and it costs one word. il faut QUE plus a subjunctive is L3's, and naming it here is what stops a later author importing the tense along with the word.

sentences.cue: Excuse me, where is the station?

words.note: A railway station. A metro stop is a station and a bus stop is an arrêt — three words where English has one.
Feminine. It is what appears on a sign with a name after it — rue de Paris — and the u is the rounded vowel.

sentences.trap: M1's Pardon is doing the opening here, and Excusez-moi would work as well. Both are ordinary; a bare Où est la gare? is not rude but is noticeably abrupt.
sentences.sound: par-DON oo eh la GAR. The où is a single oo and the r of gare is at the back of the throat.

variations.cue: Excuse me, where is the street?
Excuse me, where is the station?
Excuse me, where is the metro?

mistake.why: gare is feminine: Pardon, où est la gare?

sentences.usage: Stopping someone in the street — the module's opening move.
sentences.mnemonic: gare for trains, station for the metro, arrêt for buses.

words.note: The present tense with the pronoun taken off. Vous tournez is a statement; Tournez is an order, and nothing else has changed.
One thing, not two. There is no article inside it and none can be added — à la gauche is not what people say.
Literally a fire, and by extension a traffic light. Its plural takes an x, and au feu means at the lights.

sentences.trap: The imperative is the same word as the statement. French marks the order by dropping vous, where English changes nothing at all — so the two languages meet in the middle and the learner has to spot the difference.
sentences.sound: toor-NAY a GOHSH o FUH. The au of au feu is a pure o.

variations.display: Tournez à gauche à la gare
Prenez la première rue à gauche
variations.cue: Take the first street on the left

mistake.display: Tournez à la gauche au feu
mistake.why: The phrase takes no article: Tournez à gauche au feu.

sentences.usage: Giving directions to someone who has stopped you.
sentences.mnemonic: Drop the pronoun and you have an order.

sentences.display: Allez tout droit, puis à droite
sentences.literal: Go all straight, then to right

words.note: One thing, and one letter from droite. Straight on, not right — and the difference is the module's whole trap.
à gauche's pair, and built the same way. The te on the end is what marks it as a direction rather than "straight".
The noun. It is also the feminine of droit, which is where the confusion comes from — the words really are related.

sentences.trap: tout droit and à droite are in the same sentence on purpose. One is straight on, the other is right, and a learner who hears only droi- will go the wrong way.
sentences.sound: a-LAY too DRWA pwee a DRWAT. The t of droite is sounded and the t of droit is not.

variations.display: Allez tout droit, puis à gauche

variations.changed: a different verb — keep going rather than go

mistake.display: Allez tout droite, puis à droite
mistake.why: Straight on is tout droit: Allez tout droit, puis à droite.

sentences.usage: The first half of nearly every set of directions.
sentences.mnemonic: The t you hear is the turn.

sentences.display: Prenez le bus, puis le métro
sentences.cue: Take the bus, then the metro
sentences.literal: Take the bus, then the metro

words.note: The imperative of prendre, and it takes a bus, a street or a coffee — the same range English gives "take".
Its plural is also bus, because it ends in s. The final s IS sounded here, unusually — BÜSS.
Short for métropolitain and masculine. The é is a letter with an accent and must be written with it.
Another imperative made by dropping the pronoun. It is what a French speaker says where English says "carry on".

sentences.trap: bus sounds its final s and most French words do not. It is a borrowed word, and borrowed words keep habits French has otherwise lost.
sentences.sound: pruh-NAY luh BÜSS pwee luh may-TRO. The ü is the rounded front vowel.

variations.display: Prenez le train à la gare
variations.cue: Take the train at the station

variations.display: Continuez tout droit, puis prenez le bus
variations.cue: Keep going straight on, then take the bus

mistake.why: French keeps its articles: Prenez le bus, puis le métro.

sentences.usage: Explaining a route with more than one leg.

words.note: For anything you get INSIDE: en bus, en train, en voiture, en avion. No article follows it — en le bus is not French.
Masculine and starting with a vowel, so l'avion. en avion is by air, and the n of en links onto the vowel.

sentences.trap: No article after en. That is the whole shape — en bus, never en le bus — and it is the same instinct that gives à pied no article either.
sentences.sound: zhuh vay on BÜSS. The en is nasal and no n is actually said.

variations.changed: a vowel, and the n links onto it

mistake.why: en takes no article: Je vais en bus.

sentences.usage: Saying how you get about, which comes up early with anyone new.
sentences.mnemonic: Inside it: en. On it: à.

sentences.display: Je vais à pied, pas en voiture
sentences.literal: I go on foot, not in car

words.note: For anything you use with your body. à vélo and à moto are the same shape — you sit on them rather than in them.
The d is silent. Its plural takes an s that is also silent, so the word sounds the same however many feet are involved.
The everyday word; bicyclette is the formal one and sounds dated. à vélo, because you sit on it.

sentences.trap: The rule really is about inside and on. A bus takes en because you get in it; a bicycle takes à because you get on it — and there is no list to memorise.
sentences.sound: zhuh vay a PYAY pa on vwa-TÜR. The final d of pied is silent.

variations.display: Je vais à pied à la gare
Je vais en voiture, pas à pied

mistake.display: Je vais en pied, pas en voiture
mistake.why: You are not inside your feet: Je vais à pied.

sentences.usage: Arranging how to get somewhere, or correcting an assumption.
sentences.mnemonic: In it or on it — that is the whole rule.

words.note: It only ever appears as il faut — there is no other person of this verb in use. An infinitive follows it (tourner, prendre, aller), and nobody is named as doing the thing.
The infinitive behind Tournez. Every -er infinitive is said the same as its past participle, which is why French spelling matters so much here.

sentences.trap: The il means nothing. It is a placeholder, exactly as in il y a and il pleut, and there is no person in the sentence at all.
sentences.sound: eel fo toor-NAY a GOHSH. faut is one syllable with a pure o and a silent t.

variations.cue: You have to take the bus
You have to go straight on

mistake.why: The verb only takes il: Il faut tourner à gauche.

sentences.usage: Telling someone what has to be done, without ordering them to do it.
sentences.mnemonic: il faut has no person in it.

sentences.cue: Is it far, or is it near?

words.note: The bare adverb. L1-M7 taught près de, which names what something is near; without the de it simply means close by.
Invariable. loin de names what it is far from, and on its own it simply means a long way.
Without an accent it is "or"; with one, où, it is "where". One mark, two words, and L1-M7 owns the other.

sentences.trap: ou and où are separated only by the accent, and the accent is a letter here rather than a decoration. The index treats them as two keys, and so should the writer.
sentences.sound: say LWAN oo say PREH. The oin of loin is nasal.

mistake.why: "Or" has no accent: C'est loin, ou c'est près?

sentences.usage: The follow-up to every set of directions, and it decides whether you walk.
sentences.mnemonic: The accent turns or into where.

sentences.display: L'arrêt de bus est au coin
sentences.cue: The bus stop is on the corner
sentences.literal: The-stop of bus is at-the corner

words.note: The circumflex is a letter. l'arrêt is its own index key because the elision fuses — the same policy L1 set with l'eau.
The corner of a street, and by extension a neighbourhood — le coin means round here. Nothing to do with the English word.
A town square, a seat on a train, or room for something. Three jobs on one word, and the sentence says which.

sentences.trap: arrêt de bus has no article in the middle. Two nouns joined by de leave the second bare when it names a kind rather than a particular thing.
sentences.sound: la-REH duh BÜSS eh o KWAN. The circumflex e is open and the final t is silent.

variations.display: L'arrêt de bus est près de la gare
variations.cue: The bus stop is near the station
The station is on the corner

mistake.display: L'arrêt de le bus est au coin
mistake.why: de and le fuse into du, and here neither is wanted: L'arrêt de bus.

sentences.usage: Answering someone who asked where something is.
sentences.mnemonic: A kind of thing goes bare after de.

sentences.display: Prenez la première rue à droite
sentences.cue: Take the first street on the right
sentences.literal: Take the first street to right

words.note: The masculine premier has an acute-less e that becomes grave in the feminine — première — to keep the sound, exactly as léger did.
The ain is nasal and no n is said. en train is by rail; le train is the thing itself.

sentences.trap: première goes in FRONT of the noun, because ordinals always do. It is not on M3's list of exceptions — ordinals are a class of their own and never follow.
sentences.sound: pruh-NAY la pruh-MYEHR RÜ a DRWAT. The è of première is open.

variations.display: Prenez la première rue à gauche
variations.cue: Take the first street on the left

variations.display: Il faut prendre la première rue à droite
variations.cue: You have to take the first street on the right
variations.changed: the obligation frame instead of the order

mistake.display: Prenez la rue première à droite
mistake.why: Ordinals go in front: Prenez la première rue à droite.

sentences.usage: The precise half of a set of directions.
